author: Aesop
excerpt: The wolf saw a lamb at the stream. 'You are muddying my water!' he shouted. 'How can I, when I stand downstream´' the lamb defended itself. 'But a year ago you insulted me!' 'I was not yet born then.' 'Then it was your father!' And he devoured him. Moral: A tyrant will always find a reason for violence. The fox and the grapes: 'They are sour,' she said when she could not reach them. These animal stories are mirrors of human nature. They are brief, cruel, and true.
gem_reason: Aesop´s fables are the foundation of European didactic literature. The slave Aesop hid in them the wisdom of the oppressed ´ a realism that sees the world without embellishment. Animals represent types (cunning, stupidity, violence). The fables teach pragmatism and caution in dealing with the powerful.

author: Alain-Fournier
excerpt: Augustin Meaulnes came to our school like an apparition. One day he got lost and found a mysterious castle where a strange wedding was taking place. There he met the beautiful Yvonne de Galais. It was only a moment, a dream, but that moment determined his whole life. He returned, but the castle had vanished. He searched for it for years. When he finally found it and married Yvonne, he was not happy. Happiness exists only in longing, in searching. When a dream becomes reality, it loses its charm. Childhood is the land from which we have been expelled.
gem_reason: The author's only novel (he died in World War I) is a cult work about the loss of childhood and ideals. The atmosphere is dreamy, melancholic. Meaulnes is a romantic hero searching for the Absolute, but colliding with the banality of adulthood. It is a book about the impossibility of returning to paradise.

author: Albert Camus
excerpt: Then everything wavered. The sea exhaled a heavy, scorching breath. It seemed to me that the sky opened wide to pour down fire. My whole being tensed and I clutched the revolver convulsively. The trigger gave way, I touched the smooth belly of the grip, and then, in that dry and deafening sound, everything began. I shook off sweat and sun. I realized I had destroyed the balance of the day, the extraordinary silence of the beach where I had been happy. Then I fired four more times into the motionless body, where the bullets disappeared without leaving a trace. And they were like four short knocks on the door of misfortune.
gem_reason: Camus´s Meursault embodies existential indifference and alienation. This passage shows the author´s 'zero degree of writing' ´ terse, declarative sentences without emotional adjectives, which paradoxically intensify the brutality and absurdity of the act under the blazing Algerian sun.

author: Aldous Huxley
excerpt: And that is the secret of happiness and virtue ´ to like what you have to do. All education aims at this: to make people love their inevitable social destiny. Alpha children wear gray. They work much harder than we do, because they are so wonderfully intelligent. I am really glad I am a Beta, because I don´t work so hard. And again we are much better than Gammas and Deltas. Gammas are stupid. They all wear green and Delta children wear khaki. No, I don´t want to play with Delta children. And then there is soma, delicious soma, half a gram for a holiday from reality.
gem_reason: Huxley´s vision of the future is chilling precisely because of its 'perfection.' Society is stable thanks to genetic engineering and drugs. The style is cold, analytical, full of pseudo-scientific terms that underscore the loss of individuality in favor of collective 'happiness.'

author: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
work: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
excerpt: At five o´clock in the morning, as always, the wake-up call sounded ´ a hammer striking the rail outside the staff barracks. The broken sound struggled through the glass frozen two fingers thick and soon died away: it was cold and the guards didn´t want to ring for long. Shukhov never slept through the wake-up call, he always rose at the signal; there was about an hour and a half before roll call, his own time, not the camp´s, and who knew what could be accomplished in that time. Whoever knows the camp knows: you perish there when you start licking bowls or relying on the infirmary.
gem_reason: Solzhenitsyn´s terse, documentary style reveals the horror of the Gulag through the routine of a single day. He does not use grand words about suffering, but focuses on details of survival ´ a spoonful of porridge, a piece of bread, warmth in a boot. This banalization of evil makes the work devastating.

author: Alessandro Manzoni
excerpt: Lombardy, 17th century. Renzo and Lucia want to marry. But the local tyrant Don Rodrigo forbids it, because of a wager. The betrothed must flee. War, famine, plague. Renzo becomes entangled in riots in Milan, Lucia is abducted to the castle of the Unnamed. But Providence watches. 'God never deprives His children of joy unless He prepares a greater and surer joy for them.' The plague levels everything ´ it kills the tyrant and reunites the lovers. It is not chance, it is a plan.
gem_reason: Manzoni´s novel is a cornerstone of Italian literature (he created modern Italian). It is a historical novel, but also a religious meditation. Manzoni believes in justice, but it comes through suffering. His realism is full of gentle humor and understanding for ordinary people.

author: Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin
excerpt: My uncle, a man of honor... Onegin is a dandy, the lion of St. Petersburg salons. He is bored (spleen), educated, but superficial. He rejects the love of Tatyana, a sincere country soul, and in a senseless duel kills his friend Lensky. Years later, when he meets Tatyana again, now a married princess, he falls in love with her. But she replies: 'I love you, why deny it´ But I am devoted to another, and I will remain faithful to him until the end.'
gem_reason: Pushkin´s novel in verse (the Onegin stanza) is an encyclopedia of Russian life. Onegin is the prototype of the 'superfluous man' ´ he has means and talent, but lacks purpose. Tatyana is the moral ideal ´ choosing duty over passion. The work is a blend of irony, lyricism, and tragedy of missed chances.
